tagline.text: Leyte's spring town and the crater lakes of Mahagnao

location.label: Location
location.text: Burauen, Leyte (about 66 km southwest of Tacloban)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,000 (per person, 1 night 2 days, including transport, fees, meals and camping)

children.text: Burauen is a spring-rich town in the middle of Leyte, and Mahagnao Volcano Natural Park lies about 18 km from the town. The volcano summit, acidic lake, tropical forest trails, hot springs and a lakeside campsite are all in one place, which makes it a good pick for nature travel in inland Leyte.
Burauen is a first-class municipality in the central part of Leyte Island. It covers about
317 km²

, the town sits at about 229 m above sea level, and the highest point is 1,319 m. The 2024 census counted 54,635 residents, and there are 77 barangays. People speak Waray and Tagalog, and most are Roman Catholic. It borders Dagami, Tabontabon, Julita, La Paz, MacArthur, Albuera, Ormoc and Baybay.

Its nickname is the "Spring Capital of Leyte." Rivers and springs such as the Daguitan, Marabong, Guinarona, Malitbog and Hibuga run through the area, and thanks to the abundant water, Mahagnao Volcano Natural Park has lakes, waterfalls, mud zones and virgin forest. The park lies about 18 km from the town center at about 860 m above sea level, shares a border with La Paz, and was proclaimed a national park in 1937. Sources differ on its area, giving figures from about 341 hectares to about 635 hectares.

On the history side, Jesuit missionaries founded the settlement in 1595 as a base for mission work in central Leyte, and in 1609–1616 it was recorded as the most populous town in Leyte and Samar. In 1873 it was separated from the Dagami mission and became a town of its own. In 1916 it got the first electric system and cinema house in Leyte and Samar, and in 1962 the first rural bank in Leyte and Samar was founded. In October 1944, during the Allied liberation of Leyte near the end of World War II, it was one of the most heavily damaged towns, and in 2013 it was badly hit by Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda). An irrigation system was set up in 1912, and La Paz (1918) and Julita (1949) were later separated from Burauen.

Tourism here centers on nature and walking, not beaches or shopping. There are no large lodgings nearby, so camping in the park or staying in town is the norm. Festivals include the patronal feast on December 7–8 honoring the patron saint and Norberto Romualdez Sr. Day on June 6, along with Holy Week observances, Marian devotions and barangay fiestas. Roads, fees and visitor limits change from year to year, so please check with the Burauen tourism office or the park's operating association before you go.

Mahagnao Volcano is dormant, but because it shows thermal activity it is classified as potentially active. The summit trail is steep, with muddy sections and thorny bushes, so going with a local guide is practically required. One traveler wrote that they set out with two guides and reached the summit in about an hour. From the top you can look down on two lakes. Picking up sulfur crystals is strictly prohibited. Some visitors also report seeing Philippine macaques near the summit.

The largest lake in the park is about 16 hectares, with cottage resorts on its shore. You can go boating, kayaking and stand-up paddling, and it is also a source of seafood for residents. A rest hut on the lakeshore is described as holding 30–40 campers, with basic cooking and washing facilities.

A small lake known for its green, acidic water. It is a sanctuary for around 2,000 wild ducks of several species, and Bermuda grass that grows only in acidic soil is found on the shore. It is good for birdwatching and photography.
The smallest of the three lakes and the most remote. The trek to reach it is hard, so you need stamina and a guide. Check the route and conditions with your guide before you set out.

The park's 2022 tour guide listed two routes. The Tanguile Trail passes through forest of tanguile (a dipterocarp tree common in the area), includes a stretch you walk barefoot, and ends at Malagsum Lake. The Bulkan Trail follows a dry stream bed up to the top of the dormant volcano and looks down on two lakes, and you may see Philippine macaques. Routes and operations can change.

Calor Hot Spring is at the southern foot of the volcano and has been proposed for tourism development. A guide mentions the Maiinit hot spring in the Anonang area. The level of upkeep at both is uneven, so ask a local guide about current conditions.

Guin-aniban Falls is fed by water from Mahagnao Lake and lies a few kilometers southeast of the town. Kangunob Falls is also described as one of the falls around the park. Right after rain the volume rises and the trail gets slippery, so be careful.

blocks.title: Norberto Romualdez Sr. Park and the town

children.text: Next to the town church is the Norberto Romualdez Sr. Park, restored in June 2024. A guide also mentions a Japanese war memorial cemetery in the San Diego area, which may interest war-history travelers. Access and opening should be confirmed locally.

1 hour 30 minutes
Buy drinking water and snacks at the market, then hire a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) to Mahagnao. From town to the park is about
18 km
At the park entrance, find a guide and walk the Tanguile Trail to see Malagsum Lake. Drop your bags at the lakeside hut.
Cook and camp by Mahagnao Lake. Nights are cool, so bring a jacket.
Climb the summit with your guide on the Bulkan Trail and look down on the two lakes.
Come down, have lunch, return to town and continue to Tacloban or Ormoc.
In wetter months the summit trail is slippery and may be canceled, so leave slack in your schedule.
Take an early bus from Tacloban and a habal-habal from Burauen town to the park.
Walk the Tanguile Trail, see Malagsum Lake and eat lunch at a local eatery.
Head back into town before dark and return.
Direct flights run from Manila (NAIA) to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport, Tacloban (TAC).

. Check the fare locally.

from Tacloban to Burauen town.
Burauen and Ormoc are linked by the Burauen–Albuera road through Albuera, which connects eastern and western Leyte.
You can take a bus or van from Ormoc to Albuera and transfer to Burauen, but check timetables locally.
It is about
18 km
from town to the park, and you hire a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal). Negotiate the fare.
The road into the park was reportedly paved with concrete in 2019. An older travel account says the last stretch was covered on foot in about an hour or by four-wheel drive.
By car or rental car from Tacloban it takes about
1.5–2 hours
Check ahead whether there is parking near the park entrance.
Burauen has a tropical rainforest climate with no clear dry season. Annual rainfall is about 1,598 mm, and February to May is relatively drier. Average temperatures are about
, and May to August is the warmest stretch. The area is often affected by the northeast monsoon, tropical depressions and typhoons.

If your goal is the summit trail and camping, February–May, with relatively less rain, is recommended. June brings a lot of rain and slippery trails, and in the wet season lake levels and stream conditions can change. In any month, sudden showers can arrive, so always bring a rain jacket and a waterproof bag.

Inside the park there are lakeside huts and a campsite. A new camping area was announced in 2024, and the lakeside rest hut is said to hold 30–40 people. Hotel-type lodging has to be found in town, and the Burauen tourism office is the most reliable source for exact lodging and rates.

A 2022 report described the park's tour lunch as rice, native chicken cooked in coconut milk, local fish simmered in vinegar, fried fish and dried fish, mixed vegetables, a sweet potato roll, fruit and coconut juice. Food sold in the park is limited, so buy drinking water, snacks and camp food at the town market beforehand. Electricity in town comes from the DORELCO cooperative, and medical care includes the Burauen District Hospital and the health unit.
Always go with a local guide on the summit trail. It is steep and has thorny bushes.
The park has limited daily visitor numbers at times, so check with the tourism office or the park's Facebook page before you go.
Wear shoes that can get wet and grip well, and bring a waterproof bag and a change of clothes.
Lakeside camping can be cool at night, so bring a jacket and a sleeping bag.
Mobile signal can be weak, so download an offline map.
Hiring a habal-habal for a round trip from town to the park means you do not have to worry about the ride back.
Do not take sulfur crystals or minerals, and carry your trash back out.
Globe, Smart and DITO signal and internet work in town but may be weak in the park, so make any necessary calls in town beforehand.

At the 2022 reopening, visitors were asked to download a form from the park's Facebook page and fill it in beforehand, and daily admission was limited to 150 people (250 before the pandemic). Check whether that is still the case.
Mahagnao is dormant but has thermal activity. Do not go near steaming areas or hot ground, and follow the signs around the lakes and your guide's instructions.
Malagsum Lake is acidic and the water can irritate skin and eyes. Ask a local guide first whether swimming is possible.
After rain, trails and streams are slippery and the water level can rise suddenly.
During typhoons and heavy rain there is a landslide risk, so check weather information.
Emergency medical facilities are in town and far from the park. Bring basic medicines.
